nameStory: Yellow foxtail gets its charming name from its distinctive seed head that looks remarkably like a fox's bushy tail - especially when it catches the light with its golden-yellow bristles. The "yellow" part comes from the warm, honey-colored tint of the bristly flower spikes that shimmer in late summer sunlight. It's also called pigeon grass because city pigeons and other birds love to feast on its abundant seeds.
description: Yellow foxtail is a common annual grass that pops up just about everywhere - from sidewalk cracks to farm fields to your own backyard. This adaptable little grass grows anywhere from 8 inches to over 3 feet tall, with green to purple-tinged stems that are mostly smooth to the touch. Its most distinctive feature is the compact, cylindrical seed head that looks like a fuzzy bottle brush, usually with a yellowish glow. Though it's originally from Europe, this hardy grass has made itself completely at home throughout New England.

idTips.label: Seed Head
idTips.description: The signature feature - a dense, cylindrical spike 1-6 inches long that looks like a bottle brush or fox tail, with short yellowish bristles that feel slightly rough when you run your fingers upward against them

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, hairless leaves up to 12 inches long that have a distinctive twist or spiral pattern as they grow - run your hand along the blade and you'll feel the smooth, almost waxy surface

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Mostly hairless stems that range from bright green to having a purplish tinge, feeling smooth and slightly cool to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in clumps or patches, often tilting at angles rather than standing perfectly upright, with multiple stems arising from the base

idTips.label: Overall Texture
idTips.description: The whole plant has a relatively soft, non-scratchy feel compared to many other grasses - you can brush against it without discomfort

habitat: Yellow foxtail is the ultimate opportunist, thriving in disturbed soils throughout New England's cities, suburbs, and countryside. You'll find it in sidewalk cracks, vacant lots, garden edges, farm fields, roadsides, and anywhere the soil has been recently turned or compacted. It particularly loves sunny spots with poor to moderately fertile soil, making it a common sight around construction sites, parking lot edges, and neglected corners of yards.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small, inconspicuous grass shoots that are easily overlooked among other emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and develop their characteristic twisted leaves, with the distinctive foxtail seed heads beginning to appear by mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: The yellowish seed heads reach full maturity and become most noticeable, often persisting into early fall before the plant dies back completely.
seasonality.winter: As an annual grass, yellow foxtail dies completely, leaving only seeds behind to sprout the following year.

funFact: Yellow foxtail is such a successful seed producer that a single plant can generate over 34,000 seeds in one growing season - and those seeds can remain viable in the soil for up to 40 years, just waiting for the right conditions to sprout!
confusionNotes: Yellow foxtail is most easily confused with green foxtail, but yellow foxtail's seed head has a distinctly yellowish tint and shorter, blunter bristles, while green foxtail appears more purely green with longer, more pointed bristles. Memory trick: "Yellow foxtail = yellow tint and blunt bristles."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "weed" by many gardeners, yellow foxtail is actually an important food source for songbirds and small mammals. The "foxtail" name can be confusing because there are several unrelated plants called foxtails - this grass is different from the foxtail lilies grown in gardens or the foxtail pine trees of western mountains.
compareHints: Among New England's foxtail grasses, yellow foxtail stands out with its yellowish seed heads and relatively short, blunt bristles. Green foxtail has longer, more pointed bristles and lacks the yellow tint, while giant foxtail grows much taller (up to 6 feet) with proportionally larger seed heads. The yellow coloring and compact size make yellow foxtail the easiest of the foxtails to identify.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the foxtail family, giant foxtail stands out for its impressive size and drooping seed heads - yellow foxtail and green foxtail are much smaller with upright heads, while hooked bristlegrass has backward-pointing bristles that stick to clothing.
Among its foxtail relatives, green bristle grass stands out with its upright seed heads and completely smooth leaves.

Unlike its weedy annual relatives like yellow foxtail and green bristlegrass that prefer dry disturbed soils, knotroot bristlegrass is a wetland specialist with perennial roots and distinctive whitish-green foliage.
Among New England's foxtail grasses, hooked bristlegrass is unique for its backwards-barbed bristles that cling when touched.
Among New England's foxtail species, foxtail bristle-grass is typically the largest and most robust, with the thickest, most bottle-brush-like seed heads.
